title: There are moments in Scripture that seem small at first glance.
paragraphs: There are moments in Scripture that seem small at first glance.

A dinner.
A house.
Two sisters.
Jesus sitting in a living room while ordinary life unfolds around Him.
But underneath that quiet scene in Luke 10 is a war most believers never realize they are fighting.
Not the war between good and evil.
Not even the war between faith and unbelief.

But the war between serving Jesus…
and actually being with Him.

The war between Martha’s movement…
and Mary’s surrender.
And if we are honest, many modern Christians have built entire spiritual lives around avoiding the stillness Mary chose.
The story begins in Luke 10:38–42.
The Greek text opens with this line:
“Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν τῷ πορεύεσθαι αὐτούς…”
“Now it happened as they went…”
Jesus enters a village.

The village was Bethany.
A place that would later witness tears, resurrection, perfume poured on feet, and the grief of death itself.

But here…
before Lazarus dies…
before resurrection power shakes the tomb…
Jesus walks into a home.
Luke writes:
“A certain woman named Martha…”
The name Martha comes from the Aramaic “מַרְתָּא” (Marta).

It means:
“lady.”
“mistress of the house.”
And that detail matters deeply.
Because Martha immediately steps into responsibility.

Hosting.
Preparing.
Managing.
Serving.
Everything looked honorable.
Everything looked spiritual.
Everything looked necessary.
And that is what makes this battle so dangerous.
Because the enemy rarely tempts devoted believers away from Jesus through obvious evil first.
Sometimes he distracts them with religious activity that slowly replaces intimacy with Christ Himself.
Luke says Martha was:
“περιεσπᾶτο περὶ πολλὴν διακονίαν”

Most English translations say:
“Distracted with much serving.”
But the Greek word here is devastating.
“περιεσπᾶτο” (periespato)

It means:
dragged away.
pulled apart.
drawn in different directions.
This was not simple busyness.
Martha’s soul was being internally torn apart.
And how many believers know that feeling?

Always doing.
Always fixing.
Always producing.
Always carrying.
Always exhausted.
But internally fragmented.

Smiling publicly.
Breaking privately.

Still attending church.
Still posting verses.
Still serving ministries.
But slowly losing the ability to simply sit at the feet of Jesus without anxiety crawling inside their chest.
The tragedy is not that Martha served.
Service is holy.
The issue was that her service became louder than her surrender.
Then Scripture shifts toward Mary.
Luke writes:
“And she had a sister called Mary.”
Mary comes from the Hebrew name “מִרְיָם” (Miryam).

Scholars debate its meaning:
beloved,
rebellious,
bitterness,
wished-for child.

Yet in this moment…
Mary becomes the image of surrendered discipleship.
The text says:

“ἣ καὶ παρακαθεσθεῖσα πρὸς τοὺς πόδας τοῦ Κυρίου”
“Who also sat beside the feet of the Lord.”
This was not casual posture.
In Jewish culture, sitting at the feet of a rabbi meant discipleship.

Learning.
Receiving.
Remaining.
Mary took the position of a disciple.
And that alone was culturally shocking.
Women were rarely welcomed into formal rabbinical learning spaces in that society.
But Jesus allowed it.
Because the Kingdom of God was already overturning human pride and religious hierarchy.
Mary was not merely listening to Jesus.
She was surrendering herself to Him.
Then comes one of the most revealing phrases in the entire passage.
Luke says:

“ἤκουεν τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ”
“She was hearing His word.”
Not merely hearing sounds.
The Greek tense implies ongoing attention.
She kept listening.

While Martha’s hands were full…
Mary’s heart was open.
And eventually Martha explodes.
Because distracted souls eventually become resentful souls.
That is one of the clearest signs a believer has drifted from intimacy with God.
Resentment.

Toward others.
Toward ministry.
Toward responsibilities.
Toward people who seem “less busy.”
Martha says:

“Κύριε, οὐ μέλει σοι…”
“Lord, do You not care…?”
That sentence is heartbreaking.
Because this is where distraction eventually leads.

A person can serve Jesus so intensely…
that they begin quietly accusing Him of not caring.
Notice the progression.

Distraction became frustration.
Frustration became comparison.
Comparison became accusation.
And hidden beneath all of it was exhaustion.
Martha continues:

“εἰπὲ οὖν αὐτῇ ἵνα μοι συναντιλάβηται”
“Tell her to help me.”
In other words:

“Jesus…
make Mary become more like me.”
That spirit still exists everywhere today.

People angry at those who prioritize prayer.
People uncomfortable with deep intimacy with God.
People who secretly measure spirituality by visible productivity alone.
But then Jesus responds with astonishing tenderness.
“Μάρθα Μάρθα…”
“Martha, Martha…”
In Hebrew thought, repetition carries emotional weight.

“Abraham, Abraham.”
“Moses, Moses.”
“Samuel, Samuel.”
It signals deep affection.
Jesus was not condemning Martha.
He loved her.
And that matters because many exhausted believers secretly think Jesus only loves them when they are producing.
But Christ’s love was never earned by performance.
Then Jesus says:
“μεριμνᾷς καὶ θορυβάζῃ περὶ πολλά”
“You are anxious and troubled about many things.”
The word “μεριμνᾷς” means anxious, divided by cares.
Its root implies being mentally pulled apart.

Again…
fragmentation.
The soul split in pieces by worry.
And “θορυβάζῃ” means disturbed, agitated, inwardly noisy.
That is modern Christianity for many people.
Constant inward noise.

Notifications.
Pressure.
Image management.
Endless content.
Ministry branding.
Performative spirituality.
Emotional exhaustion hidden behind inspirational captions.

Many believers are physically near Jesus…
while internally miles away from resting in Him.
Then comes the line that pierces through centuries.
“ἑνὸς δέ ἐστιν χρεία”
“But one thing is necessary.”
One thing.
Not twenty.
Not endless striving.
Not proving yourself.
One thing.
Jesus continues:

“Μαριὰμ γὰρ τὴν ἀγαθὴν μερίδα ἐξελέξατο”
“For Mary has chosen the good portion.”
The phrase “good portion” carries covenant language.
In the Old Testament, God Himself was often called someone’s “portion.”
Psalm 73:26 in Hebrew says:
“צוּר־לְבָבִי וְחֶלְקִי אֱלֹהִים לְעוֹלָם”
“God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.”
Mary was not merely choosing silence over work.
She was choosing God Himself as her inheritance.
That is the battle.
Not laziness versus discipline.
Not responsibility versus irresponsibility.

The real battle is whether Jesus remains the center…
or whether ministry, survival, productivity, and distraction slowly replace Him while still using His name.
Martha’s danger was not wickedness.
It was nearness without surrender.
And that is terrifying because it can happen inside churches every single day.

People preaching without prayer.
Serving without intimacy.
Leading without abiding.
Singing without worshiping.
Posting about Jesus without sitting with Him.
The Greek word for “abide” in John 15 is:
“μένω” (menō)

It means:
remain.
stay.
dwell.
continue.
Not visit occasionally.
Remain.
And modern believers struggle deeply with remaining.

Silence feels uncomfortable.
Stillness feels unproductive.
Waiting feels weak.
But the Kingdom has always functioned differently than the world.
In Hebrew thought, presence mattered more than performance.
That is why Psalm 46:10 says:
“הַרְפּוּ וּדְעוּ כִּי־אָנֹכִי אֱלֹהִים”
“Be still and know that I am God.”

The phrase “הַרְפּוּ” (harpu) literally means:
let go.
release.
stop striving.
Many people cannot hear God clearly because their inner world never becomes quiet enough to recognize His voice.

And eventually…
activity becomes a hiding place.
Some serve constantly because silence would expose how spiritually dry they actually feel.
Some stay endlessly busy because stillness would force them to confront grief, sin, fear, addiction, loneliness, or the emptiness they keep outrunning.
But Mary sat down.
And surrender always begins there.
At His feet.

Not building your own kingdom.
Not curating your image.
Not proving your worth.
Just Jesus.
This is also why Jesus later says in John 6:27:

“μὴ ἐργάζεσθε τὴν βρῶσιν τὴν ἀπολλυμένην”
“Do not labor for food that perishes…”
Christ was constantly redirecting people from temporary obsession toward eternal reality.
Because eventually every accomplishment fades.

Every platform fades.
Every applause fades.
Every earthly identity fades.
But intimacy with Christ remains eternal.
And there is another layer hidden in this story many overlook.
Martha welcomed Jesus into her house.
But Mary welcomed Jesus into her attention.

One can host Him externally…
while resisting Him internally.
That is why surrender feels threatening.
Because true surrender means Jesus has the right to interrupt your pace, your plans, your identity, your ambitions, your habits, your schedule, and even your version of spirituality.
Mary surrendered control.
Martha maintained control.

One rested.
One managed.

One listened.
One performed.

One chose presence.
One chose pressure.
And Jesus said only one was necessary.
Not because service is evil.
But because intimacy must always come first.
Otherwise service eventually becomes self-powered religion instead of Spirit-filled obedience.
This is why so many believers burn out.
They try to carry what only intimacy with Christ can sustain.
The early church understood this deeply.
In Acts 6, when ministry demands increased, the apostles said:
“We will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.”
The Greek word for “devote” is:
“προσκαρτερήσομεν”

It means steadfast continuation.
Persistent adherence.
Refusing to drift away.
Prayer was not secondary support work.
It was survival.
Because no public ministry can remain spiritually healthy while private intimacy with God is dying.
And maybe that is the hidden ache in many hearts right now.
Not lack of information.
Not lack of sermons.
Not lack of Christian content.
But lack of communion with Jesus Himself.

Many know about Him…
while rarely slowing down enough to truly be with Him.
And Christ is still speaking the same invitation.
Come sit.
Come listen.
Come rest.
Come surrender.
Not because responsibilities disappear.
But because peace is only found at His feet.

The world teaches:
produce more.

Jesus says:
abide in Me.
The world rewards noise.
God often speaks in whispers.
The world glorifies exhaustion.
Jesus says:
“Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek word for rest there is:
“ἀναπαύσω”

Refresh.
Restore.
Give intermission from burden.
Not temporary distraction.
True soul rest.
And that rest only comes through Him.

Not success.
Not ministry.
Not productivity.
Not online validation.
Not religious performance.
Only Christ.
Maybe that is why this little story still unsettles hearts thousands of years later.
Because most people see themselves in Martha before they ever become like Mary.
The good news is that Jesus loved Martha enough to confront her gently.
And He still does the same today.

Not to shame exhausted believers…
but to call them back to the “one thing necessary.”
Himself.

If your soul has become noisy…
fragmented…
restless…
numb…
Maybe this is your invitation to stop running for a moment and return to the feet of Christ again.
Not for performance.
Not for appearance.
But for real communion.
Because no amount of serving Jesus can replace actually knowing Him.
And someday, when every distraction dies and eternity stands unveiled before us, the only thing that will matter is whether we truly remained near to Him.
